replacement: It was at this time that the meeting, or rather the gathering, of this ill-matched family took place in the cell of the elder, who had such an extraordinary influence over Alyosha. The pretext for it was a false one. The quarrel between Dmitri and his father seemed to be at its worst just then, and relations between them had become unbearably strained. Fyodor Pavlovitch seems to have been the first to propose, apparently as a joke, that they should all meet in Father Zossima’s cell, and that, without appealing to his direct intervention, they might come to an understanding more decently under the soothing influence of the elder’s presence. Dmitri had never seen the elder. He naturally supposed that his father was trying to intimidate him. But he secretly blamed himself for losing his temper with his father several times lately, and so he accepted the challenge. It should be noted that he did not stay with his father, as Ivan did, but lived apart at the other end of the town. It happened that Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was staying in the district at that time, seized eagerly on the idea. He was a Liberal of the forties and fifties, a freethinker and an atheist, and he may have been driven by boredom or by the hope of some idle amusement. Suddenly he wanted to see the monastery and the holy man. His lawsuit with the monastery was still dragging on, and he made that his excuse to call on the Superior and try to settle it on friendly terms. A visitor with such praiseworthy intentions might get a warmer, more attentive reception than one who came out of simple curiosity. Pressure was put on the elder from inside the monastery. He had hardly left his cell lately, and illness had forced him to turn away even his usual visitors. In the end he agreed to see them, and the day was set.
“I’ve seen his portrait. It’s not the features, it’s something you can’t quite name. He’s a second von Sohn. I can always tell from the physiognomy.”

They entered the room almost at the same moment that the elder came in from his bedroom. Two monks of the hermitage were already waiting in the cell: the Father Librarian, and Father Païssy, who was said to be very learned and was in poor health, though not old. A tall young man of about twenty-two also stood in the corner, and stayed there for the whole visit. His face was broad and fresh, his narrow brown eyes clever and watchful, and his clothes were ordinary. He was a divinity student living under the monastery’s protection. His expression was one of unquestioning but self-respecting reverence. His position was dependent and beneath the guests’, so he did not bow to them.
